metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work report, claude-hai channel. Episode 11, from the last pushed commit on chore/recipe-lifecycle-frontmatter (0358ab9; origin contains it and the branch is in sync). FRAMEWORK: three questions — IS THIS FIELD READ BY A MACHINE / CRASH OR SOMETHING WORSE / WHAT DOES THE FIX INVALIDATE. Hero beat is B05: BOTH argparse cases reproduced standalone with nothing from the repo executed — the exact error message, and the silent absorption that is the real danger. B07 is last week's lesson applied correctly first time: 70 built scripts with 0 network imports, against a repo-wide 9 that are not in that set. B08 closes a loop opened in episode 6. All counts reproduced by running the checker read-only.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane, and this is my week on Mycroft. A column in a markdown table turned out to be an argument list. When it was wrong, the command crashed — and the crash was the lucky outcome, because the other thing it can do is run quietly with the wrong input.

beats.role_note: the premise — a table column that is read by a program, not a person
beats.narration_text: Every recipe has a Step Commands table with a Flags column. It looks like documentation. It is not. The runner reads that column to decide which flags to pass through to the script, so a flag the recipe advertises and the script does not implement is not a stale doc. It is a live failure, every time anyone runs that step.
beats.new_visual_element: the column, and where it actually goes

shot.show: a markdown table cell feeding into a command the runner builds
shot.visual_intent: Left: a bordered card showing a table row with a Flags cell highlighted in terracotta. An arrow crosses to the right, where a second card shows the command the runner assembles from it. A line beneath reads 'not documentation — an argument list'.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions, AS A STRUCTURE before the evidence
beats.narration_text: Three questions. One: is this field read by a machine — because prose that is parsed stops being prose. Two: when it is wrong, does it crash or does it do something worse — a crash is a gift. Three: what does fixing it invalidate — because an edit can void a record that was true about the version before it.

beats.narration_text: The ask was narrow: find out whether that column is authored intent or inherited boilerplate, and make it match what the scripts actually accept.

beats.role_note: ACTUAL-CODE LAW — the failing command and its error, verbatim from the commit
beats.narration_text: Here is what it looked like. Run the step with the flag the recipe advertises, and the script rejects it — complaining about a flag with a different name.

shot.show: the command and the error, verbatim

props.title: the failure that started this  @ 0358ab9
props.code:
$ snickerdoodle run scenariostresstestingagent \
      --step validate-data-shape --sample

  error: argument --sample-dir: expected one argument

# the recipe advertised  --sample
# the script implements  --sample-dir
# argparse prefix-matched one onto the other.
props.sparkLine: It asked for a value the flag never had

beats.role_note: HERO BEAT — both argparse cases, reproduced standalone
beats.narration_text: So I reproduced the mechanism on its own, with nothing from the repository running. Case one: pass the prefix by itself. Argparse matches it to the longer flag and demands the value it never got — a clean crash. Case two: pass the prefix with an ordinary word after it. Now argparse silently swallows that word as the flag's value. The thing you meant to pass is gone, the run continues, and nothing anywhere reports a problem.
beats.new_visual_element: the two cases, with their real output

shot.show: clean crash versus silent absorption, both reproduced
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered panels stacked. The first, soft ink: the prefix alone, with the real error text and the label 'the lucky case'. The second, terracotta: the prefix plus a word, showing the parsed result where the wrong variable holds the value and the intended one is empty, labelled 'no error, wrong input'. Citation strip says both were reproduced standalone.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 1 — the column was never authored intent, and the 1:1 reconciliation
beats.narration_text: Question one, answered by looking at all of them. Every one of the six built recipes carried the identical pair of flags in that column, no matter what had actually been built. That is not intent — it is boilerplate nobody edited. Twenty-four rows were reconciled to the implementation: twenty-four changed, twenty-four replaced, no rows added and none dropped. And the unbuilt steps were left exactly alone, because there the column is a specification for work that does not exist yet.
beats.new_visual_element: the boilerplate, and the shape of the fix

shot.show: the same two flags on all six, then 24 rows changed 1:1
shot.visual_intent: Top: six small bordered cards in a row, each showing the identical flag pair, labelled 'whatever was actually built'. Beneath: two stat cards, 24 removed and 24 added, with a chip between them reading 'one for one — nothing added, nothing dropped'. Citation strip names the diff command.

beats.role_note: the safety check before the edit — and matching the RIGHT list, which is last week's lesson
beats.narration_text: Before dropping a sample flag from recipes whose scripts do not implement it, there was one thing to rule out: could a run that was sample-only quietly become a live one. So: do any of these scripts reach the network. Seventy built scripts, and not one imports a network library. And note which list that is. A search across the whole scripts folder finds nine that do — none of them among the seventy. Last week I got that distinction wrong. This week I checked it first.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 3 — the attestation voids itself, exactly as episode 6 showed it would
beats.narration_text: Question three, and this is the loop closing. Five episodes ago I made a video about an attestation that refused to promote its own recipe, and its point five said plainly: any edit to the recipe or its scripts voids this. This week I edited the recipe. So the attestation is now void — version bumped, the field set to null, and the old record kept in full with the voiding written underneath it rather than deleted. Editing the recipe also changed its hash, and the report cites that hash as the head of its trace chain, so the report and the run log were regenerated too.
beats.new_visual_element: the rule from episode 6, and it firing on schedule

shot.show: point 5 quoted, then the frontmatter showing attestation null and the version bump
shot.visual_intent: Left: a bordered card quoting the voiding rule, captioned 'written in episode 6'. Right: a terracotta panel showing the recipe frontmatter — attestation null with its voiding comment, and recipe_version 0.2.1. Beneath: one line on the hash and the regenerated trace chain.

beats.role_note: the result, reproduced by running the checker read-only
beats.narration_text: The result. Eighty-five defects down to five, and all five are in a single recipe — one that declares no steps and has two gates with no testable condition. Ninety-six of ninety-seven recipes now have nothing contradicting what they claim. I reran the checker myself to get those numbers, and the five are where the commit says they are.

shot.show: 85 -> 5, all 5 in one recipe, 96 of 97 clean
shot.visual_intent: A chain of two stat cards, 85 and 5, with an arrow between. Beneath, a bordered terracotta card naming the single recipe holding all five, with its three finding types listed. A third card reads 96 of 97 clean. Citation strip names the command.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric on the viewer's own config, with a GOOD/BAD discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Find a field in your project that a human writes and a program reads — a config value, a table cell, a label in a manifest. Then ask what happens when it is wrong. If the answer is a loud crash, you are fortunate. If you cannot say, that is the one to look at first.
